research_tasks: Read the long-form first-person interviews this run located but did not review, transcribing each fully and labelling speakers (pitch separation worked for the Bloomberg film): ABC News full interview with Rebecca Jarvis (YouTube qUDG06BvWxc, 2026-02-07, 23:36); CNBC Television interview (GMXnmaky9FY, 2026-01-03, 36:24); Anthropic's 'Building Anthropic | A conversation with our co-founders' (om2lIWXLLN4, 2024-12-20, 51:49), the only located source where named co-founders may describe her; 'A conversation with Dario Amodei & Daniela Amodei' (Claude channel, 7xco5Qd2Oo8, 2026-05-06, 33:10); 'The Co-Founders of Claude AI Tell Oprah' (w5dJqHilu5s); Bloomberg Live 'Anthropic President Amodei on the Future of Claude' (Kfz-NxEvu-U); Sixth Street conversation (iTaHatJKphg). In each, look for her own account of what she does under pressure, what she says she was protecting in costly choices, how she disagrees with Dario, and any named colleague describing her.

Obtain and read The Information's 'Anthropic's "First Lady" Took a Winding Road to the Top' (2026-08-13, S27) through a subscription or library; record every named Stripe, OpenAI and Anthropic colleague's testimony with locators. It is likely the only long profile built on named testimony about her.

Re-open The Atlantic excerpt (S12) from a fresh, verifiable copy (or Kevin Roose's book The AGI Chronicles) to confirm the paragraphs quoted from the 2026-10-05 capture, and record the context of her 2023 interview with Roose about the stuffed-animal council.

Test a discriminator among Two, Six and One against the new material: when she explains her own costly choices (leaving Stripe, the 2018 language-project standoff, leaving OpenAI, leading the 2020 negotiations, withholding Mythos), does she cite the people she was protecting or serving (Two), the trustworthiness and safety of the group and the downside she feared (Six), or what was right and fair (One)? Separately, in conflict, does she move toward repair and other people's feelings, toward procedure and rules, or toward allies and guarantees? Record at least two dated, sourced observations on each side before choosing.

Seek on-record accounts of the WSJ and Atlantic OpenAI episodes (S12, S13): Brockman's 2020 peer review and her point-by-point rebuttal, the Altman conference-room confrontation, the Murati clash. Check whether Anthropic or Daniela has responded, and whether Brockman or Murati has spoken on record. Until then they stay 'disputed' and cannot carry the type argument.
Find named testimony from her Stripe years (she credits Claire Hughes Johnson as a mentor and model) and from Anthropic executives about how she manages conflict, feedback and pressure.

Read the paywalled The Times interview (2024-06-26, S26) and TIME's May 2024 'Inside Anthropic' feature for any first-person motive statements; verify Wikipedia leads before use (Lowell High School; August 2017 wedding month).

Decide format only after the tasks above: her public career dates to 2021-2023 (FLI podcast March 2022; TIME100 AI September 2023), so open-case eligibility ('first breakout within roughly three years; record thin because it is young') is borderline at best. If a defensible discriminator still does not exist after the reading above, put the eligibility question to DJ and the verifier explicitly rather than defaulting to an open case to meet the reported Nov. 9 roadshow date.

Current accuracy before drafting: re-check IPO status after the reported Oct. 14, 2026 investor event and any public S-1 (her titles, board-chair role, equity, any super-voting shares), and update Forbes figures with a date.

sources.title: Daniela Amodei Says Curiosity Is Underrated (Stanford GSB View From The Top, podcast page with full transcript)
sources.speaker: Daniela Amodei, interviewed by Gintare Zukauskaite (Stanford GSB); page by Michael McDowell

sources.locator: Opened by direct fetch (HTTP 200) on 2026-10-06 and the full transcript read end to end. Key passages: original-career-plan answer ('I graduated in 2009'; 'defining feature, of both me and Dario'); generalist answer ('What is this lady actually good at?'; 'something that feels really wrong to me'); leaving-OpenAI answer ('big sip of water'; 'a lot of integrity'; 'running towards something'); co-founder answer ('fighting and getting over it for almost 40 years'; vacation test); AI-safety answer ('radical responsibility'; 'eating disorders for teenage girls'); AI use-cases answer ('I'm a career manager'; 'People love people'; upward feedback; 'two little kids'); bubble answer ('we could absolutely be wrong'); rapid-fire (literature; Thanksgiving; weekly time outside the office; Guns of August); best-advice answer (mentor: 'You already know what the right answer is'). The page notes the transcript is automated and lightly edited.
sources.excerpt: So I was like, “Okay, there’s something that feels really wrong to me about the fact that I was born in America, I had access to all of the sort of basic things that we take for granted in life.” / I’m a career manager. So I spend most of my time with people ... everybody thinks that AI is not going to come for their job, because they’re so special, and I am extremely guilty of this. I was like, “People love people. People are going to want to report to me. They’re not going to want to report to Claude, obviously.” / So I upload all of my reports, upward feedback for me, and sometimes Claude will kind of very kindly be like, “It sounds like you haven’t improved on this in the past year. Maybe you should get some extra coaching, Daniela.” / So for example, Dario and I have been fighting and getting over it for almost 40 years. Because he’s my brother, and I used to steal his toys, right? / We were like, “This is kind of a crazy thing to do. Maybe we should stay. Maybe we could make this work.” But we talked, I talked to one sort of friend and mentor outside of work, and she was like, “Honestly, I don’t think you really need to be on the phone with me. You already know what the right answer is.” / I’m gonna take a big sip of water, for that one. / And I think, in our own very different ways, all seven of us are people that have a lot of integrity. / But I think to us, the kind of highest level of framing, is just taking a form of radical responsibility for the technology that we’re developing. / I actually think developers who created these technology companies, they weren’t like, “I’m setting out to cause a pandemic of eating disorders for teenage girls.” / So we build in time every week when we hang out outside of the office. / Sometimes we’re able to say things to each other that nobody else in the company can. / It’s ultimately a bet. ... but we could absolutely be wrong. / But I think it’s a really important study of just the individual people and personalities that resulted in, and sort of led to, the beginnings of what became World War I. / I have two little kids. So I have an almost-five-year-old, and an almost-one-year-old. / Sometimes Claude is wrong. Heretical to say, but a fact. / I would probably major in literature again. I know that sounds crazy. I like to read.
sources.context: The longest first-person source in the record: a friendly live interview before business-school students, so self-presentation, humor and Anthropic messaging all shape it. Strong on how she describes herself; silent on what she personally fears or resents. The co-founder material repeats what Fortune summarized (not re-opened this session), so cite this transcript, not Fortune. Children are mentioned only as context; do not name or describe them.

sources.excerpt: Dario and I have always been really close. I think since we were very, very small, we've always had this special bond around really wanting to make the world better or wanting to help people. So originally started my career in international development ... and part of why I got interested in that is that it was an interest area of Dario's at the time ... I was very keen to understand the things that he was working or interested in as a potential area to have impact. / we both started donating small amounts of money to organizations that were working on global health issues like malaria prevention when we were still both in school. / I worked in Washington DC at a few different NGOs, I spent time working in east Africa for a public health organization, I worked on a congressional campaign, I've worked on Capitol Hill, so I was much more in this classic, like a friend at an old job used to call me, the classic do-gooder. / So I think for me, I've always been someone who has been fairly obsessed with trying to do as much good as I personally can, given the constraints of what my skills are and where I can add value in the world.
sources.context: Earliest long interview in the record, recorded about a year after founding and before commercial success, in a friendly effective-altruism-adjacent venue. Valuable as a pre-fame baseline: the do-good motive language matches the 2026 GSB talk four years later. Joint interview with Dario, so some answers are shaped by the pairing.

And I also hold a high bar. Those are kind of the two things I hear the most. ... In terms of things I'm less good at, probably unsurprisingly, I'm not the expert in anything / But my default there was, you guys are gonna have to talk about it and figure it out either way, right? And so when I saw the opportunity at OpenAI and I knew people there / And I actually write a document at the beginning of every year saying, here's what we should expect from just a pure scaling perspective over the next year at Anthropic, because I've seen it before, right? / But there are some customers who come to us and the honest conversation we have with them is, I don't think we can do anything for you right now. sources.excerpt: Daniela Amodei has an energy that's hard to place — warm, unhurried, immediately present. She swept into a sunlit room on the ground floor of Anthropic's headquarters in December, sat down, and immediately apologized for her mug. / "Is my, like, gigantic novelty mug going to be distracting if I have it?" she said. "I'll defer to the wise camera people in terms of what's in the shot." / "One of the values and the things that we talk about a lot internally is just how not to believe the hype," Daniela Amodei told CNBC. "For us, it's never been about seeking attention or sort of being in the headlines. We're really here to do the work." / "Dario and I really help each other," she added. "He's great at pushing me to think about the big picture... sources.title: If Anthropic Succeeds, a Nation of Benevolent AI Geniuses Could Be Born (Wired)
sources.speaker: Steven Levy (Wired), quoting Daniela Amodei, Dario Amodei, Amanda Askell and others
sources.locator: Opened by direct fetch (HTTP 200) on 2026-10-06; the Daniela passages located and read in context: family paragraph ('In the 1970s, their parents'); high-school paragraph (flute scholarship; 'saved the world'); OpenAI-arrival paragraph ('Joan Didion fangirl'; GPT-2 'Daniela was managing the team'); founding paragraph (January 2021 tent photo); effective-altruism paragraph ('outdated term'); constitutional-AI paragraph.
sources.excerpt: In the 1970s, their parents, Elena Engel and Riccardo Amodei, moved from Italy to San Francisco. Dario was born in 1983 and Daniela four years later. Riccardo, a leather craftsman from a tiny town near the island of Elba, took ill when the children were small and died when they were young adults. Their mother, a Jewish American born in Chicago, worked as a project manager for libraries. / Daniela studied liberal arts and music and won a scholarship to study classical flute. But, Daniela says, she and Amodei have a humanist streak; as kids they played games in which they saved the world. / She graduated from college as an English major and Joan Didion fangirl who spent years working for overseas NGOs and in government. ... Daniela was managing the team. / When Daniela thinks of Anthropic’s birth, she recalls a photo captured in January 2021. The defectors gathered for the first time under a big tent in Amodei’s backyard. ... Everyone was wearing Covid masks. Rain was pouring down. / Ask Daniela about it and she says, “I’m not the expert on effective altruism. I don’t identify with that terminology. My impression is that it’s a bit of an outdated term.” Yet her husband, Holden Karnofsky, cofounded one of EA’s most conspicuous philanthropy wings, is outspoken about AI safety, and, in January 2025, joined Anthropic.
sources.context: Long-form magazine profile with office access; centered on Dario. The parents paragraph is Levy's narration; it does not name the father's illness or town. Wikipedia's 'Massa Marittima' is not supported here (and the Dario run found Wikipedia's Italian citation does not support it either): use 'a tiny town near the island of Elba'. No first-person statement from Daniela about her father's death was found; do not build a childhood-wound argument.

sources.title: OpenAI vs. Anthropic: Inside the Biggest Rivalry in Tech (The Atlantic; adapted from The AGI Chronicles)
sources.speaker: Kevin Roose (The Atlantic), quoting Daniela Amodei (2023 and 2026 interviews) and unnamed OpenAI employees and people who know the Amodeis
sources.locator: A fresh fetch on 2026-10-06 hit a CAPTCHA (reader proxy) and WebFetch is blocked for the domain. The full text was read this session from the reader-proxy capture of the gift-link URL made on 2026-10-05 by the Dario run (3,687 words). Paragraphs used (capture numbering): 20 (Brockman toast at her 2017 wedding; Murati clash); 21 ('high-EQ counterpart'; 'inflexible triumvirate'); 22 (stuffed-animal advisory council; 2023 quote); 23 ('Dario's clique'); 29-30 (BATNA; 'the divorce'; she led negotiations; mutual non-disparagement); 43 ('stressful on every dimension'); 44-45 ('despise', anonymous; 'power-hungry virtue-signalers', anonymous OpenAI critics). Re-verify against a fresh copy before quoting.
sources.excerpt: His sister, Daniela Amodei, was also getting fed up with OpenAI. She and Brockman had once been close. (Brockman even gave a toast at her 2017 wedding to Holden Karnofsky, who joined OpenAI’s nonprofit board that year.) But years of working together had strained their relationship. She had also started to clash with Mira Murati, then OpenAI’s vice president of applied AI and partnerships, over who was in charge of making decisions related to safety. / Inside OpenAI, some employees viewed Daniela as her brother’s high-EQ counterpart. She was a skilled manager who had majored in English literature in college and worked in politics before her career in tech. But as her role expanded to include managing more of OpenAI’s technical teams, she collided with Brockman and other leaders, who came to see her as the third member of an inflexible triumvirate that included Dario and Karnofsky. / Daniela had an unusual process for working through conflicts. She and Karnofsky had a large collection of stuffed animals, which they treated as their personal advisory council for managerial role-playing. Each animal had an assigned character profile. Jinji was a lazy cat who encouraged Daniela to cancel meetings and avoid taking on too much work. Maura, a pink bear, was a detail-oriented, type-A manager. A panda named Beary Bonds was the “patron bear of generosity and empathy.” She treated these exercises as something between an inside joke and an earnest management technique. (In 2023, she told me the animals were “very useful in analyzing different personality types.”) / Daniela Amodei, who was leading the negotiations on the BATNA group’s side, asked to take some of their internal research documents with them to the new company. They agreed to sign a mutual non-disparagement agreement / “It’s stressful on every dimension,” Daniela told me. “And it’s scary because we can lose it at any time. That’s just on the business side. Then there’s the mission, and we’re like, Are we accidentally making things worse? Like, we think we have all the safety stuff figured out, but do we?” / Dario and Daniela still despise Altman and Brockman, according to several people who know them well. / In private, some people at OpenAI have described the Amodeis as power-hungry virtue-signalers, not principled humanitarians.
sources.context: Book excerpt by a named reporter. Her two direct quotes are on record. Most narration (the clashes, 'high-EQ counterpart', 'triumvirate', 'despise', the critics' line) rests on unnamed sources and is contested; Roose and the WSJ (S13) are separate bylines but may share sources, so treat them as partially independent. The mutual non-disparagement agreement is a circumstantial explanation for her public restraint about OpenAI. Breitbart (S28) and Inc. are derivative of this piece, not corroboration.

sources.excerpt: Daniela’s fiancé, Holden Karnofsky , also lived in the group house. / Living together in the group house, Dario, Daniela and Karnofsky had shared both a commitment to AI safety and a sense of whimsy. Daniela was such a fan of her stuffed animals that Karnofsky had proposed to her via a movie of the dolls coming to life. Dario wore a panda outfit to their costume party-themed wedding. His clique at OpenAI became known as “the pandas.” / Brockman recruited Daniela to OpenAI, where she became a jill-of-all-trades, working on engineering management and recruiting. She had married Karnofsky, who was on the OpenAI board, the prior year. / Daniela, who was co-leading the language project with Radford, told Brockman he couldn’t work on it. When Altman asked her if there was any way to make it work, she offered to step down as head of the project rather than allow Brockman on it. / Altman called Dario and Daniela into a conference room and accused them of plotting against him by encouraging colleagues to send negative feedback about him to the board. The brother and sister denied it. ... Daniela called that executive into the room, who said she had no idea what Altman was talking about. Altman then denied that he had said it, prompting the Amodeis to begin shouting angrily at him. / Brockman wrote a lengthy piece of feedback for Daniela accusing her of abusing her power to create bureaucratic processes to get her way. He showed it to Altman beforehand, who declared it “tough but fair.” Daniela delivered a long response, rebutting him point by point. / Daniela was ultimately tapped to lead the exit negotiations with their lawyers.
sources.context: Investigative reporting relying largely on unnamed sources from both camps; Daniela is not quoted giving her side of any episode. Every interpersonal episode is reported and contested: attribute to the WSJ, do not present private feedback or the shouting as established fact, and do not use them alone to type her. Syndicated copy, not independent corroboration of the WSJ.

sources.excerpt: Dario and I, we've always been really close since we were little. But I think we always really wanted to do something big together. / He was so smart. He was taking, you know, calculus when he was, you know, in, I think, like middle school. He took math classes at UC Berkeley when he was in high school. I was actually more into reading and arts. So we were almost like complete complements in that way. / I think when people interact with Claude versus, you know, other systems, there is more of a feeling of, I like to describe it as professional warmth. So the goal is not for it to be your best friend, but it's not for it to be sort of cold, rote, calculating. It should feel approachable, but distant, right? Professional. / The example I often reach for is what will happen in medicine. ... They can't have a bedside manner with you that says, tell me how you're feeling about this. How are you coping with going through this process? ... But the interpersonal human part, that's not going to change. / I think we've tried to be as publicly open as possible to say we're trying our best to make this decision well, but we might not do it perfectly. / It was really scary to read that. I mean, it was, we were obviously extremely relieved that he and his family were okay. ... I hope that this is a topic we can all just debate, you know, as peacefully as possible. / We view it as our job to try and proactively think about all of the things that could go wrong. Because if we don't, who's going to? / We should not just say, well, we were just trying to grow the product, and suddenly there's an entire generation of young women who have eating disorders or who have mental health problems because, whoops, we were just trying to grow the product. That's not the stance that I think any technology company should take. (narration, ~4:04: 'They lived together in San Francisco, along with Daniela's husband, Holden Karnofsky.')
sources.context: Edited documentary; answers may be cut and reordered. The medicine and eating-disorders answers repeat the GSB talk (S01) nearly verbatim, so they are stable talking points, not spontaneous disclosures. The Altman-home answer is a conciliatory public statement about a rival she reportedly clashed with privately (S12, S13).

claims.claim: Daniela Amodei was born in 1987 in San Francisco, four years after Dario (born 1983), and the siblings grew up in the Mission District. Birth year only; no full birth date is supported. Forbes listed her age as 39 in 2026.
claims.inference: Stable biographical frame. Supports birth year and birthplace metadata only.
claims.alternative: No source gives a full birth date; never render 1987 as January 1. Wikipedia's birth year cites the same Wired passage, so it is not independent.

claims.claim: Her parents, Elena Engel (a Jewish American born in Chicago who worked as a project manager for libraries) and Riccardo Amodei (a leather craftsman from a tiny town near the island of Elba), moved from Italy to San Francisco in the 1970s; Riccardo took ill when the children were small and died when they were young adults.
claims.inference: Family background only. No source in the record has Daniela describing her father's illness or death or linking it to her choices.
claims.alternative: Do not name the town (Wikipedia's 'Massa Marittima' is unsupported, S25) and do not build a childhood-wound explanation; nothing in her own words supports one.

claims.claim: She studied liberal arts and music in high school, won a classical-flute scholarship, majored in English literature at UC Santa Cruz (the Stanford eCorner introduction says English Literature, Politics, and Music), graduated in 2009, was a Joan Didion fan, and says she would major in literature again.
claims.inference: A humanities path into a technical field; she credits the humanities for her people-management approach (S04).
claims.alternative: The eCorner degree wording is the host's introduction; Forbes and Wired say English literature. Keep the major as English literature.

claims.claim: Before tech she worked in international development and global health (NGOs in Washington, DC; time in East Africa for a public-health organization), helped win a 2012-cycle congressional campaign in northeast Pennsylvania, and spent a few months on Capitol Hill running scheduling and communications for Rep. Matt Cartwright.
claims.inference: Consistent account across her own interviews (2022, 2024, 2026) and independent Business Insider reporting.
claims.alternative: The campaign year is inferred from Cartwright's election and is not stated by these sources; state it only as 'a congressional campaign in northeast Pennsylvania' unless verified.

claims.claim: She left Capitol Hill quickly: 'this is extremely not for me ... It just was slow and bureaucratic and I missed the campaign days of getting to build something together with a small group of, you know, motivated people.'
claims.inference: A costly early exit toward small, committed teams building together; the same preference reappears in her Stripe (40 people) and Anthropic (seven co-founders) choices.
claims.alternative: Ordinary early-career fit-finding; one self-report, told years later in a talk urging students to follow their passions.

claims.claim: She joined Stripe in 2013 when it had about 40 people, as an early recruiter, later moving into risk; she left in 2018. She gives different leaving headcounts: 'around 1200' (2023) and 'from 40 to 1500' (2024).
claims.inference: Career facts for the timeline; the move from recruiting to risk shows a people-and-safety thread that Business Insider also notes (S08).
claims.alternative: Do not state a precise Stripe headcount at departure; her own figures differ.

claims.claim: On leaving Stripe she said: 'I loved Stripe ... it was a hard decision to leave,' because payments 'didn't sort of feel like fully meeting this other aim ... positively impact the world,' and she went to OpenAI where 'I knew people there'; the WSJ reports Greg Brockman, a friend from Stripe, recruited her.
claims.inference: A costly move justified by impact, made through existing relationships. Fits a do-good motive (One or Two) and a preference for trusted people (Six or Two).
claims.alternative: Common career logic for an early employee after five years; the recruitment detail is WSJ reporting from unnamed sources.

claims.claim: At OpenAI (2018-2020) she worked across engineering management and recruiting, managed the team that built GPT-2 ('I oversaw the team that did GPT2'), co-led the language project with Alec Radford, and became vice president of safety and policy.
claims.inference: Establishes that she managed technical teams, not only operations.
claims.alternative: The 'co-led the language project' detail is WSJ reporting; the VP title rests on Fast Company and the Stanford introduction.

claims.claim: She describes a lifelong closeness with Dario built around wanting to make the world better: 'Since we were kids, we've always felt very aligned' (2023); as children they played games in which they saved the world (Wired); 'we always really wanted to do something big together' (2026). Dario independently says they 'decided very early' to work together.
claims.inference: A stable, repeated self-account (2022-2026) with family corroboration; the sibling bond is central to the portrait.
claims.alternative: Public sibling narratives are also brand-useful for Anthropic; both siblings have reasons to present harmony. The WSJ and Atlantic portray them as a tight unit in conflict at OpenAI (S12, S13), which is consistent.

claims.claim: Her move into international development followed Dario's interest: 'it was an interest area of Dario's at the time ... I was very keen to understand the things that he was working or interested in'; as students they both donated small amounts to malaria-prevention groups.
claims.inference: An early instance of orienting her path around a loved person's concerns: consistent with a Two's attunement to others, a Six's alignment with a trusted figure, or simply shared values.
claims.alternative: She was a younger sibling in college; following an admired older brother is common and may say little about core motive.

claims.claim: She frames her motive as doing good: a friend called her 'the classic do-gooder'; 'I've always been someone who has been fairly obsessed with trying to do as much good as I personally can, given the constraints of what my skills are and where I can add value in the world' (2022); 'there's something that feels really wrong to me about the fact that I was born in America ... How do I make that more fair?' (2026).
claims.inference: The same motive language four years apart, before and after fame. 'Feels really wrong' and 'fair' lean One; 'add value' and helping lean Two.
claims.alternative: This is also the shared vocabulary of the effective-altruism milieu she moved in (GiveWell, Open Philanthropy) and of Anthropic's mission messaging, so it may reflect culture as much as type.

claims.claim: She has repeatedly defined her job as translating Dario's vision rather than setting it: 'I personally think Dario is the most impressive technical visionary in this space ... I really view my job as helping to take that vision ... and help to actually translate it into sets of operating norms' (2023); he thinks in 5-10 years, she in 1-2 (2023); 'I'm much more sort of practical' (2024). Dario: 'my job is the second and Daniela's job is the first' (operational execution). By June 2026 every executive except Dario's chief of staff reported to her.
claims.inference: A durable, chosen supporting role beside a visionary while holding most of the managerial power. Fits a Two (indispensable partner, power behind the visible leader) or a Six (loyal lieutenant to a trusted authority).
claims.alternative: A rational division of labor between a researcher and an operator; she herself frames it as comparative advantage (S01). Holding all executive reports and the board chair (C35) is real power, which also fits a non-Two reading.

claims.claim: She locates her own value in people wanting her: 'I'm a career manager. So I spend most of my time with people ... everybody thinks that AI is not going to come for their job, because they're so special, and I am extremely guilty of this. I was like, "People love people. People are going to want to report to me. They're not going to want to report to Claude, obviously."'
claims.inference: The most Two-shaped statement in the record: she names the belief that she is indispensable to people, and names it as a flaw.
claims.alternative: A humorous aside in an answer about AI and jobs; one statement, not a pattern. Self-aware joking about pride does not establish a core motive.

claims.claim: She reports that her direct reports most often describe her as both 'a supportive manager. I really want people to succeed' and someone who 'hold[s] a high bar', and says she is 'not the expert in anything'.
claims.inference: Her own summary of others' feedback. 'Supportive' and 'want people to succeed' fit Two; 'high bar' fits One. It does not discriminate between them.
claims.alternative: Second-hand (her report of reviews), delivered to students; managers commonly describe themselves this way.

claims.claim: She uses Claude to read three to four years of performance reviews to spot recurring patterns in her reports, and uploads her own upward feedback, quoting Claude 'very kindly' telling her she hasn't improved on something in a year.
claims.inference: Investment in other people's development plus openness to criticism. Consistent with a supportive manager; also with a One's improvement drive or a Six's appetite for external checks.
claims.alternative: Also a product demonstration by Anthropic's president.

claims.claim: When two technical leaders reporting to her disagreed, her default was to push them to resolve it: 'I probably shouldn't even be the arbiter. I should just sort of be supporting you in figuring that out.'
claims.inference: A supportive, non-directive conflict style when she lacks expertise; leans Two or Nine.
claims.alternative: Sensible practice for a non-technical manager of researchers; contrasts with the reported OpenAI fights (C19-C21), where she did not stay out.

claims.claim: Inside OpenAI, some employees viewed her as Dario's 'high-EQ counterpart' and 'a skilled manager'; as her role grew she collided with Brockman and other leaders, who came to see her as part of an 'inflexible triumvirate' with Dario and Karnofsky.
claims.inference: Outside perception of emotional attunement (supports Two) and of rigidity under conflict (supports One or Six), from the same unnamed sources.
claims.alternative: Unnamed employees, filtered through a reporter writing about a feud; the 'triumvirate' view comes from her adversaries.

claims.claim: She and Karnofsky kept a collection of stuffed animals used as a 'personal advisory council' for managerial role-playing: Jinji, a lazy cat who urged her to cancel meetings; Maura, a detail-oriented, type-A pink bear; Beary Bonds, the 'patron bear of generosity and empathy.' In 2023 she told Kevin Roose the animals were 'very useful in analyzing different personality types.' The WSJ separately reports Karnofsky proposed via a movie of the dolls coming to life and Dario wore a panda outfit to their costume-themed wedding.
claims.inference: A playful but earnest method of externalizing competing voices and other people's perspectives before conflicts. It can read as empathic role-taking (Two), as an externalized inner committee consulted for guidance (Six), or as whimsy. Two separate reporting lines describe the animals.
claims.alternative: Roose says even OpenAI colleagues who knew weren't sure how seriously she took it. Now circulating as ridicule in partisan media (S28); treat with respect and do not over-read a private habit.

claims.claim: The WSJ reports that, while co-leading OpenAI's language project, she told Brockman he couldn't work on it and offered to step down as head of the project rather than allow him on it; Altman asked her to stay.
claims.inference: If accurate, a costly stand to protect a team's composition (and her brother's position): protective loyalty (Two or Six) or principle (One), but also a power move.
claims.alternative: Unnamed sources; she is not quoted; Radford reportedly felt his preferences were used in a proxy war. Use only as attributed, contested reporting.

claims.claim: The WSJ reports that in 2020 Brockman wrote peer feedback accusing her of 'abusing her power to create bureaucratic processes to get her way' (Altman called it 'tough but fair'), and that she rebutted it point by point; The Atlantic reports she clashed with Mira Murati over who decided safety matters.
claims.inference: The strongest counterevidence to a soft-helper reading: fights over decision rights and process. Process as leverage fits One or Six; fierce defense of her domain also fits a Two under threat.
claims.alternative: An adversary's characterization during a feud, reported from unnamed sources; she has not publicly answered it.

claims.claim: The WSJ reports that when Altman accused Dario and her of encouraging negative feedback about him to the board, she called the executive he cited into the room, that executive denied it, Altman then denied saying it, and the Amodeis shouted at him.
claims.inference: If accurate: she checked the facts in the room, then reacted with open anger to a perceived lie. Anger at dishonesty fits One (and Six's sensitivity to betrayal).
claims.alternative: Single report, unnamed sources, no response from her; sensitive. Do not present as fact or use alone to type her.

claims.claim: She led the departing group's side of the exit negotiations with OpenAI at the end of 2020 (the group called it 'the divorce'), asked to take some internal research documents, and both sides signed a mutual non-disparagement agreement.
claims.inference: Two reporting lines agree she was the negotiator. The non-disparagement agreement is a circumstantial explanation for her diplomatic public silence about OpenAI.
claims.alternative: S12 and S13 may share unnamed sources; the document request and the agreement come from S12 alone.

claims.claim: Before leaving OpenAI she hesitated ('This is kind of a crazy thing to do. Maybe we should stay. Maybe we could make this work.') and called a friend and mentor, who told her, 'You already know what the right answer is.' She calls it the best advice she has received.
claims.inference: Sought outside counsel before a high-stakes break and recalls being told to trust herself: Six-shaped (seeking guidance, doubting own authority) or ordinary prudence.
claims.alternative: Told as a lesson to students; seeking counsel before leaving an employer with a large group is normal.

claims.claim: In public she consistently says the founders were 'running towards something versus running away from something,' takes 'a big sip of water' before answering why they left, and TIME described both siblings as 'diplomatic' about it; privately, according to The Atlantic's unnamed sources, the Amodeis 'still despise Altman and Brockman.'
claims.inference: A gap between public restraint and reported private animus. Could show image management, harmony-keeping, or simply the non-disparagement agreement (C22).
claims.alternative: The 'despise' line is anonymous and contested; the restraint has a contractual explanation.

claims.claim: Her co-founder advice centers on testing relationships before committing: 'the interpersonal relationships ... matter a lot more than you think. How do you guys have conflict together?'; 'Dario and I have been fighting and getting over it for almost 40 years'; 'go on vacation together ... Share a room with them.'
claims.inference: Trust-testing before commitment (Six) and relational emphasis (Two).
claims.alternative: Widely shared founder advice; Anthropic's seven co-founders were long-known colleagues, so the advice describes her circumstance.

claims.claim: She and Dario schedule weekly time together outside the office to 'water that relationship', and say things to each other 'that nobody else in the company can.'
claims.inference: Deliberate relationship maintenance; Two- or Nine-consistent, also simply healthy practice for sibling co-founders.
claims.alternative: Rapid-fire answer, partly joking ('Thanksgiving dinner').

claims.claim: She speaks openly about doubt and pressure: 'It's stressful on every dimension ... scary because we can lose it at any time ... Are we accidentally making things worse?' (2026); 'We're doing our best ... we don't necessarily know what the right answer is' (2026); AI 'is ultimately a bet ... we could absolutely be wrong' (2026); on Mythos access, 'we might not do it perfectly' (2026).
claims.inference: Repeated anxious vigilance and doubt: the Six case's best first-person support.
claims.alternative: Her company sells caution and is preparing an IPO; doubt is mission-aligned and investor-appropriate messaging, and Dario says similar things. Work incentive may explain it.

claims.claim: She frames safety as responsibility for harm to people: 'radical responsibility'; social-media founders did not set out 'to cause a pandemic of eating disorders for teenage girls'; 'whoops, we were just trying to grow the product. That's not the stance that I think any technology company should take'; 'if we don't, who's going to?'
claims.inference: Moral responsibility (One) expressed through concern for vulnerable people (Two). Repeated nearly verbatim across venues, so a settled talking point.
claims.alternative: Company positioning against social media and rivals; repetition shows message discipline, not necessarily inner motive.

claims.claim: She says Anthropic tells some would-be customers 'I don't think we can do anything for you right now. And we don't wanna sell you a bill of goods ... to close a deal with you and get your logo.'
claims.inference: Integrity in sales; One-leaning.
claims.alternative: Also a sound enterprise sales strategy and part of Anthropic's 'honest' branding.

claims.claim: She repeatedly argues human relationships become more valuable as AI improves, using 'the example I often reach for' of doctors' bedside manner.
claims.inference: A consistent worldview centered on interpersonal care; Two-consistent.
claims.alternative: A stock answer to the jobs question at an AI company.

claims.claim: She is persistently self-deprecating: 'What is this lady actually good at? She doesn't have a law degree. She's not a computer scientist'; a mock memoir title 'I Need an Adult'; Anthropic 'messed up' payroll 'multiple times'; her themed-days schedule has a '70% hit rate'; 'Sometimes Claude is wrong. Heretical to say.'
claims.inference: Ease with her own imperfection and humor about status; weighs against a tense, self-critical One presentation and against a Three's image focus.
claims.alternative: Self-deprecation is also a disarming public style for a powerful executive.

claims.claim: She says Anthropic is about 'how not to believe the hype ... it's never been about seeking attention or sort of being in the headlines,' yet she fronted the company's first Super Bowl campaign interviews in February 2026.
claims.inference: Stated aversion to attention; weighs against a Three image motive.
claims.alternative: Corporate messaging; fronting the ad is part of her job.

type_hypothesis.against: The best-documented conflicts (C19-C21, reported from unnamed sources) show her fighting over control of projects, processes and decision rights rather than seeking closeness; Brockman's reported charge that she used 'bureaucratic processes to get her way' and her point-by-point rebuttal read as One or Six as easily as a Two defending her people. Her most repeated motive language is fairness, responsibility and doing good (C11, C28, C29), which fits One. The warmth evidence is largely executive self-presentation in a people-and-operations role at a company whose brand is 'professional warmth', and several key lines are repeated talking points (C28, C30). The record contains almost no first-person account of her own needs, resentments, or what she fears for herself, which is where Two, Six and One would separate. Her own feedback summary ('supportive manager ... high bar', C14) straddles Two and One.
type_hypothesis.alternative_case: A Six reading fits a cluster of choices: she tests co-founders' trust before committing (C25) and built Anthropic from a long-trusted in-group; she sought a mentor's counsel and voiced 'maybe we should stay' before leaving OpenAI (C23); she writes an annual document anticipating what scaling will bring (S04); she repeatedly voices doubt and fear of loss ('scary because we can lose it at any time ... Are we accidentally making things worse?', C27); her stuffed-animal 'advisory council' externalizes competing voices she consults before conflicts (C18); and the reported anger at Altman's denial (C21) fits sensitivity to betrayal. Type 1 is a second live alternative: 'something that feels really wrong ... How do I make that more fair?' (C11), 'radical responsibility' and moral anger at growth-at-all-costs (C28), integrity in sales (C29), a self-reported 'high bar' (C14), and reported reliance on process (C20). Weighing against Six: she moves decisively and repeatedly toward risky small ventures (C05, C06, C07) and her doubt statements are mission- and investor-appropriate. Weighing against One: her relaxed, self-deprecating ease with mistakes (C31).
type_hypothesis.discriminator: No defensible discriminator yet. The candidate test: in her own accounts of costly choices and conflicts, what does she say she was protecting? People she serves and her place with them (Two), the safety and trustworthiness of the group against a feared downside (Six), or what is right and fair (One)? The current record mixes all three (C07 cites impact and 'I knew people there'; C23 cites doubt and outside counsel; C05 cites building with a small, motivated group; C19-C21 are third-hand). The only sharply Two-shaped first-person line (C13) is a single joke. The unread long-form interviews and The Information profile are the most likely places to settle it.
type_hypothesis.unexplained: Why a self-described supportive, high-EQ manager became, in two independent reports, the hard-edged negotiator and process-enforcer of the OpenAI split (C19-C22); why she distanced herself from effective altruism so flatly despite her husband's role in it (C33); how 'I hold a high bar' coexists with her easy self-mockery (C14, C31); and how much of the public warmth is temperament versus the role Anthropic needs her to play beside Dario.
